claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu coatings form a disordered FCC solid solution at room temperature.
The room-temperature FeNiCrCoCu coating has high lattice distortion.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has inherent spatial heterogeneity in stacking-fault energy.
Lattice-parameter differences among constituent elements generate friction that hinders partial-dislocation motion and causes hardening.
Severe local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and strengthens high-entropy alloys.
At low temperature, lattice friction in FeNiCrCoCu promotes stable work hardening through partial-dislocation dissociation and stacking-fault formation.
Increasing temperature reduces the Peierls barrier and lattice friction in FeNiCrCoCu.
Thermal activation causes a transition from sessile to mobile partial dislocations, stacking-fault widening, rapid dislocation glide, and cross-slip.
At a critical temperature, the rate of dislocation multiplication exceeds the rate of dislocation annihilation or lattice ordering.
Proliferating partial dislocations and stacking faults coalesce into an amorphous-like, low-viscosity shear band.
Shear-band formation and local lattice disorder cause rapid material removal and unstable wear.
The critical transition temperature for FeNiCrCoCu is approximately 500–600 K.
Wear resistance and elastic modulus decline sharply above the critical temperature.
The elevated-temperature transition changes the dominant wear mode from abrasive wear to severe adhesive or oxidative wear.
Stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at 300 K arise from lattice-distortion strengthening and controlled dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic FCC HEAs with moderate-to-high stacking-fault energy and lattice-friction-dominated room-temperature strengthening.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to precipitation-hardened systems or BCC alloys without substantial thermal softening.
The cited evidence does not provide a critical transition temperature for FeNiCrCoCu.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says the high-temperature shear band bypasses defect-mediated plasticity, whereas the mediator and mechanism describe rapid proliferation and evolution of dislocations and stacking faults as the direct route to that shear band. The intended distinction between bypassing defect-mediated plasticity and defect-triggered disorder is not clearly defined.
